## 9. Two enlargements of the attack surface, closed

### 9.1 A cycle count for arbitrary self-maps

To compare families of permutations we need a uniform notion. For an arbitrary $f : \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ define the *iteration orbit* $\mathcal{O}_f(x) = \{f^{[k]}(x) : 0 \le k < N\}$ and let $C_f$ be the number of distinct sets $\mathcal{O}_f(x)$, $x \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For a permutation of an $N$-element set every orbit closes within $N$ steps, so $C_f$ is the honest cycle count; and for $f = \sigma_a$ one recovers $C_f = C(N,a)$.

**Lemma 9.1 (conjugation invariance).** If $e$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ with $e \circ f = g \circ e$, then $C_g = C_f$.

*Proof sketch.* Induction gives $g^{[k]}(e(x)) = e(f^{[k]}(x))$, so $\mathcal{O}_g(e(x)) = e(\mathcal{O}_f(x))$; the map $S \mapsto e(S)$ is injective on subsets and carries the family of $f$-orbits bijectively to the family of $g$-orbits. $\square$

### 9.2 Affine maps

**Theorem 9.2 (invisible shift).** Let $\gcd(a,N)=1$ and suppose $1 - a$ is invertible modulo $N$. Then for every $b$,
$$C\bigl(x \mapsto ax+b\bigr) \;=\; C(N,a).$$

*Proof.* Let $c = b(1-a)^{-1}$, so $ac + b = c$. The translation $e(x) = x + c$ satisfies $e(ax) = ax + c = a x + ac + b = a(x+c) + b$, i.e. $e \circ \sigma_a = \sigma_{a,b}\circ e$ where $\sigma_{a,b}(x)=ax+b$. Apply Lemma 9.1. $\square$

**Theorem 9.3 (pure translation).** For $b \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, the translation $x \mapsto x+b$ has exactly $\gcd(N,b)$ cycles, all of length $N/\gcd(N,b)$.

*Proof sketch.* Every orbit is a coset of the cyclic subgroup generated by $b$, whose order is $N/\gcd(N,b)$; the number of cosets is $\gcd(N,b)$. $\square$

The general case interpolates between these two extremes, and the answer is a single gcd.

**Theorem 9.4 (classification of the affine readout).** Let $A$ be a unit of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ and put $g = \gcd\bigl(N,\ A - 1\bigr)$. Then for all shifts $b, b'$,
$$\gcd(g, b) = \gcd(g, b') \implies C\bigl(x\mapsto Ax+b\bigr) = C\bigl(x\mapsto Ax+b'\bigr).$$
In particular $C(x \mapsto Ax+b) = C(N,A)$ whenever $g \mid b$, and Theorem 9.2 is the case $g=1$.

*Proof sketch.* Two conjugations act on the family $\sigma_{A,b}$: rescaling by a unit $u$ (i.e. $e(x)=ux$) sends $\sigma_{A,b}$ to $\sigma_{A,ub}$, and translating by $t$ sends $\sigma_{A,b}$ to $\sigma_{A,b+(A-1)t}$. Hence the cycle count is a function of the orbit of $b$ under $b \mapsto ub + (A-1)t$, $u \in (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$, $t \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. Bézout's identity realises $g$ inside the ideal generated by $A-1$ and $N$, and a standard computation shows that this orbit is exactly $\{b' : \gcd(g,b') = \gcd(g,b)\}$. Lemma 9.1 finishes. $\square$

**Interpretation.** Enlarging the family $x \mapsto ax$ (one parameter) to $x \mapsto ax + b$ (two parameters) buys exactly one additional gcd probe, $\gcd(N, a-1, b)$ — polynomial-time computable without any factorisation. The affine readout adds nothing.

**Theorem 9.5 (affine sign law).** For every $N$, every $a$ coprime to $N$, and every shift $b$,
$$N - C(x\mapsto ax+b) \;\equiv\; \bigl(N - C(N,a)\bigr) + \bigl(N - \gcd(N,b)\bigr) \pmod 2 .$$
That is, $\mathrm{sign}(\sigma_{a,b}) = \mathrm{sign}(\sigma_a)\cdot\mathrm{sign}(x\mapsto x+b)$.

*Proof sketch.* Use the general fact that a permutation $\pi$ of a finite set $X$ has $\mathrm{sign}(\pi) = (-1)^{|X| - \#\mathrm{orbits}(\pi)}$, together with multiplicativity of the sign: $\sigma_{a,b} = \tau_b \circ \sigma_a$ where $\tau_b(x)=x+b$. Theorem 9.3 supplies $\#\mathrm{orbits}(\tau_b) = \gcd(N,b)$. $\square$

**Corollary 9.6.** At an odd modulus $N$ the shift never affects the sign — for $N$ odd, $N - \gcd(N,b)$ is even iff $\gcd(N,b)$ is odd, which always holds — so $\mathrm{sign}(\sigma_{a,b})$ equals $J(a\mid N)$ for every $a$ and every $b$: again factorisation-free.

### 9.3 Power maps

**Theorem 9.7 (power readout at a prime).** Let $p$ be prime and $k \ge 1$ with $\gcd(k, p-1)=1$, so that $x \mapsto x^k$ is a permutation of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Then
$$C\bigl(x \mapsto x^k \ \text{on } \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\bigr) \;=\; C\bigl(p-1,\ k\bigr) \;+\; 1 ,$$
the right-hand count being that of the *multiplication* permutation $y \mapsto ky$ of $\mathbb{Z}/(p-1)\mathbb{Z}$.

*Proof sketch.* Fix a primitive root $g$ mod $p$. The discrete logarithm is a bijection $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \to \mathrm{Option}\bigl(\mathbb{Z}/(p-1)\mathbb{Z}\bigr)$ sending $0$ to the extra point and $g^y$ to $y$; under it $x \mapsto x^k$ becomes $y \mapsto ky$ with the extra point fixed. Orbit counts are invariant under conjugation by a bijection, and adjoining a fixed point adds exactly one orbit. $\square$

So the power readout is the multiplicative readout **one level down**, at the modulus $p-1$. Since $p-1$ is even, Theorem 8.7 applies verbatim and yields:

**Theorem 9.8 (power-map sign law).** For an odd prime $p$ and $k \ge 1$ with $\gcd(k,p-1)=1$, the permutation $x \mapsto x^k$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is even if and only if
$$4 \mid p-1 \implies k \equiv 1 \pmod 4 .$$

Once more the sign is explicit and factorisation-free.

## 10. Algorithms

We record the procedures implicit above, with their costs.

**Algorithm A (stratified cycle count).** *Input:* $N$, $a$ with $\gcd(a,N)=1$. *Output:* $C(N,a)$.
For each divisor $d$ of $N$, compute $M = N/d$, then $\varphi(M)$ and $\operatorname{ord}_M(a)$, and accumulate $\varphi(M)/\operatorname{ord}_M(a)$. Cost: $\tau(N)$ order computations. Note this is a *predictive* formula for someone who already knows the factorisation of $N$; it is not available to an adversary.

**Algorithm B (brute-force readout).** *Input:* $N$, $a$. *Output:* the multiset of cycle lengths.
Mark all elements unvisited; for each unvisited $x$, walk $x, ax, a^2x, \dots$ until returning to $x$, marking as you go and recording the length. Cost: exactly $N$ map applications and $O(N)$ memory. This is the honest cost of the readout for someone without the factorisation, and it is the content of barrier 5.2.

**Algorithm C (factoring from an informative point).** *Input:* $N = pq$, a multiplier $a$ primitive at $q$, and a point $x \in S_p$. *Output:* $q$.
Walk the cycle through $x$ and return (length $+ 1$). Correct by Theorem 4.2 — but note that Theorem 5.1 makes the *input* $x$ already a factorisation of $N$: the algorithm is correct and useless.

**Algorithm D (Burnside cross-check).** *Input:* $N$, $a$. *Output:* verification of (6.1).
Compute $L = \operatorname{ord}_N(a)$ and $\sum_{k<L}\gcd(N,a^k-1)$ by repeated squaring and Euclid; compare with $L\cdot C(N,a)$. Cost $O(L \log^2 N)$. Any $k$ with $1 < \gcd(N,a^k-1) < N$ is a successful Pollard probe.

**Algorithm E (free sign prediction).** *Input:* $N$, $a$. *Output:* the parity of $N - C(N,a)$.
If $N$ is odd, return "even" iff $J(a\mid N)=1$ (reciprocity, $O(\log^2 N)$); if $N$ is even, return "even" iff ($4 \nmid N$ or $a \equiv 1 \bmod 4$). Correct by Theorem 8.8. Cost: polynomial, no factorisation. This algorithm predicts a global invariant of a permutation on $N$ points without ever touching the permutation.

---

## 11. Numerical illustrations

**$N = 143 = 11\cdot 13$, $a=2$.** $\operatorname{ord}_{143}(2)=60$, $\operatorname{ord}_{11}(2)=10$, $\operatorname{ord}_{13}(2)=12$. Strata: $|S_1|=120$ with $2$ cycles of length $60$; $|S_{11}|=12$ with one cycle of length $12$; $|S_{13}|=10$ with one cycle of length $10$; $|S_{143}|=1$. Total $C=5$, matching (4.1). Burnside: $60\cdot 5 = 300 = \sum_{k<60}\gcd(143, 2^k-1)$, the sum consisting of $143$ (at $k=0$), nine hits of value $11$ or $13$, and the rest $1$ — each hit a successful Pollard probe (e.g. $k=10$ gives $11$, $k=12$ gives $13$).

**$N=65$, $a=57$ vs $b=31$.** $\operatorname{ord}_{65}(57)=\operatorname{ord}_{65}(31)=4$; unit-stratum data identical. $C(65,57)=17$, $C(65,31)=20$. The readouts differ; the lcm does not. Signs: $65-17 = 48$ even and $J(57\mid65)=+1$; $65-20=45$ odd and $J(31\mid65)=-1$ — Theorem 8.6 in action.

**Excess.** $N=13\cdot 17$, $a=7$: $\operatorname{ord}_{13}(7)=12$, $\operatorname{ord}_{17}(7)=16$, $i_p=i_q=1$, $\gcd=4$; (7.1) predicts $2\cdot 2 + 3 = 7 = C(221,7)$.

**Affine.** $N=15$, $A=4$: $g=\gcd(15,3)=3$. Shifts with $\gcd(3,b)=3$ give $9$ cycles (the multiplicative value), shifts with $\gcd(3,b)=1$ give $3$ — exactly two classes, as Theorem 9.4 requires. For $A=2$, $g=1$ and all $15$ shifts give the same count $5$.

**Power maps.** $p=13$: $k=5$ gives $9$ cycles $=C(12,5)+1$; $k=7$ gives $10 = C(12,7)+1$. Since $4 \mid 12$, the sign law says $x\mapsto x^k$ is even iff $k\equiv 1 \pmod 4$: indeed $k=1,5$ are even permutations and $k=7,11$ odd.

**Cost.** For $N=3127=53\cdot59$ the enumeration touches all $3127$ points ($\varphi(N)=3016$ of them units), while $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor = 55$; informative points number $111$, density $0.036 \le 6/\sqrt{N} \approx 0.107$. For $N = 34571 = 181\cdot 191$: $34571$ points versus $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor = 185$, informative density $0.011$.

## 12. Discussion

### 12.1 What kind of barrier is this?

The usual vocabulary of cryptographic hardness — one-wayness, unstructuredness, generic-group lower bounds — does not describe the situation here. The secret is not hidden by the object: the cycle structure of $\sigma_a$ *displays* $\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ and $\operatorname{ord}_q(a)$ separately and permits reading $q$ off a single cycle by a subtraction. The obstruction is that the object is an enumeration of $N$ elements whose informative region is exactly the set of points that already constitute a factorisation. One might call this an **access barrier** rather than an information barrier: the information is present, exact, and cheap to interpret, but the apparatus for viewing it costs $\Theta(N)$ and its interesting sub-apparatus is inaccessible by construction.

This suggests a sharper way to formulate hardness claims for order-based attacks: not "the readout is symmetric" (it is not) but "every polynomial-time-accessible functional of the readout is computable from $(N,a)$ alone". Sections 6, 8 and 9 verify exactly this for the natural candidates: the cycle count is a Pollard aggregate; the sign is a Jacobi symbol (odd $N$) or a residue condition mod $4$ (even $N$); the affine extension adds one gcd; the power maps are the same readout one level down.

### 12.2 Placement in the order-probe hierarchy

The results complete a natural three-step characterisation of multiplicative orders as an attack resource:

* **Free as probes.** Anything computable inside $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is available to the adversary — but by (1.1) it is lcm-flattened.
* **Partial as constraints.** Order information constrains the smooth parts of $p-1$ and $q-1$, which is what Pollard's $p-1$ exploits; Theorem 6.3 shows the cycle count is precisely the aggregate of those constraints and improves on them only when they already succeed.
* **Sealed as readouts.** The ring-level permutation does separate the individual orders (Theorem 4.1) and does factor (Theorem 4.2), yet is sealed behind the three barriers of Section 5 and the freeness results of Sections 8–9.

### 12.3 Positive by-products

Although the cryptanalytic verdict is negative, several statements are of independent interest:

* The stratification law (Theorem 3.5) is a clean closed form for the cycle type of multiplication on a general residue ring, and specialises to a divisor-sum formula for prime powers (Corollary 3.7).
* Theorem 8.6 is a Zolotarev–Frobenius theorem for arbitrary odd moduli, proved by parity localisation over strata; Theorem 8.7 completes it at even moduli, where the phenomenon that the sign forgets the odd part of $N$ entirely seems worth advertising.
* Theorem 9.4 is a complete classification of the affine cycle count in terms of a single gcd, and Theorem 9.7 identifies the power-map readout at a prime with the multiplicative readout at $p-1$.

---

## 13. Future directions

1. **A barrier-4 lower bound.** Prove unconditionally that *any* algorithm extracting an individual prime order from the ring-level readout requires $\Omega(N)$ operations, in a model that captures "iterating the permutation" without presupposing a specific implementation. The Burnside identity (6.1) suggests the right currency: what an algorithm can learn cheaply is a partial sum of Pollard probes.
2. **A quantum channel.** Period-finding samples group structure without enumerating it. Is there a quantum procedure whose measurement statistics see the *stratified* structure — the individual $\operatorname{ord}_{N/d}(a)$ — rather than only the global $\operatorname{ord}_N(a)$? The strata are not subgroups, so the standard hidden-subgroup framework does not directly apply.
3. **Hint amplification.** All barriers here are for the uniform, hint-free setting. If an adversary is given a weak hint about $p$ or $q$ (a few bits, an approximation, a smoothness promise), does the stratified readout amplify it? Theorem 5.3's density bound is the quantitative statement to beat.
4. **Beyond affine and power families.** The two enlargements analysed here collapse to the multiplicative readout. Are there permutation families of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, still cheap to specify, whose cycle structure is *not* conjugate to a multiplicative one and not a readout one level down?
5. **General moduli and higher-degree strata.** The excess formula (7.1) is stated for two prime factors. What is the exact surplus for $N$ with $r$ prime factors, and is there an inclusion–exclusion form of the "only the gcds are new" principle?
6. **Signs of other arithmetic permutations.** Theorems 8.8 and 9.8 give complete sign laws for multiplication, affine maps and power maps. The same parity-localisation technique should apply to further natural families (e.g. Möbius transformations on the projective line over $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$), each time asking whether the resulting invariant is factorisation-free.

---

## 14. Conclusion

The permutation $x \mapsto ax$ of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ has a completely determined cycle structure: strata indexed by the divisors of $N$, with sizes $\varphi(N/d)$ and uniform cycle lengths $\operatorname{ord}_{N/d}(a)$. For a semiprime this separates the two prime orders into distinct cycle lengths, defeating the lcm-blindness that limits unit-group probes, and yields a correct factoring algorithm. It is nonetheless useless: informative points are themselves factorisations, the enumeration costs more than trial division, individual cycle lengths are order-finding problems, the cycle count is an aggregate of Pollard probes that beats its floor only when a probe already wins, the surplus over the lcm is exactly one gcd, and every coarse summary — the sign at any modulus, the affine extension, the power maps — is computable in polynomial time from $N$ and $a$ alone. The asymmetric readout exists, is exactly understood, and is sealed.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The lcm-blindness of order probes}

Almost every algorithm attacking integer factorisation through multiplicative
structure ultimately manipulates \emph{orders}. For $N=pq$ a product of two
distinct primes and $a$ coprime to $N$, the Chinese Remainder Theorem gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lcm}
  \ord_N(a)=\lcmop\bigl(\ord_p(a),\ \ord_q(a)\bigr).
\end{equation}
An adversary ignorant of $p$ and $q$ may still compute freely inside the unit
group $(\ZN)^\times$; but every quantity so obtained is a function of
$\ord_N(a)$ and hence, by \eqref{eq:lcm}, a \emph{symmetric} function of the two
prime orders. We call this loss \textbf{lcm-blindness}.

It is natural to ask whether some canonical object attached to $a$ and $N$
escapes the flattening. We study the most elementary candidate: the permutation
\[
  \sigma_a:\ZN\to\ZN,\qquad \sigma_a(x)=ax,
\]
of the \emph{whole ring}. Because $\sigma_a$ also moves the non-units, it is
strictly finer than any unit-group probe and, as we show, separates $\ord_p(a)$
from $\ord_q(a)$ completely.

\section{Setting and notation}

Throughout $N\ge1$ and $\gcd(a,N)=1$. We write $\varphi$ for Euler's totient;
$\ord_M(a)$ for the least $k\ge1$ with $a^k\equiv1\pmod M$ (with
$\ord_1(a)=1$); $J(a\mid N)$ for the Jacobi symbol at odd $N$; and
$i_M=\varphi(M)/\ord_M(a)$ for the \emph{index} of $a$ at modulus $M$.

\begin{definition}
$\sigma_a:\ZN\to\ZN$, $\sigma_a(x)=ax$. Since $a$ is invertible, $\sigma_a$ is a
bijection.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
For $d\mid N$ the \emph{stratum} is $S_d=\{x\in\ZN:\gcd(x,N)=d\}$. The strata
partition $\ZN$; $S_1$ is the unit group and $S_N=\{0\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{period} of $x$ is the least $k\ge1$ with $a^kx\equiv x\pmod N$; its
cycle is $\{a^kx:k\ge0\}$. We write $C(N,a)$ for the number of cycles.
\end{definition}

Since $\gcd(ax,N)=\gcd(x,N)$, each stratum is $\sigma_a$-invariant.

\section{The stratification law}\label{sec:strat}

\begin{lemma}[modulus reduction]\label{lem:core}
For $N\ge1$ and integers $x,m\ge0$,
\[ N\mid mx \iff \frac{N}{\gcd(N,x)}\ \Big|\ m. \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $d=\gcd(N,x)$, $N=dN'$, $x=dx'$ with $\gcd(N',x')=1$. If $N\mid mx$ then
$dN'\mid mdx'$, so $N'\mid mx'$ and coprimality gives $N'\mid m$. Conversely if
$m=N'c$ then $mx=N'c\,dx'=N(cx')$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[stratified period law]\label{thm:period}
For $\gcd(a,N)=1$, $x\in\ZN$ and $k\ge0$,
\[ a^kx\equiv x \pmod N \iff \ord_{N/\gcd(N,x)}(a)\mid k. \]
In particular the period of $x$ is $\ord_{N/\gcd(N,x)}(a)$, depending on $x$
only through its stratum.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The congruence says $N\mid(a^k-1)x$, equivalent by Lemma~\ref{lem:core} to
$M\mid a^k-1$ with $M=N/\gcd(N,x)$, i.e.\ to $a^k\equiv1\pmod M$. As $M\mid N$,
$a$ is invertible mod $M$, so this holds iff $\ord_M(a)\mid k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:size}
For $d\mid N$, $|S_d|=\varphi(N/d)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$x\mapsto x/d$ is a bijection from $S_d$ onto the units of $\Z/(N/d)\Z$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:cycles}
For $d\mid N$ the stratum $S_d$ is a disjoint union of cycles all of length
$\ord_{N/d}(a)$, and their number is $c_d=\varphi(N/d)/\ord_{N/d}(a)=i_{N/d}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[cycle count]\label{thm:count}
For $\gcd(a,N)=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:count}
  C(N,a)=\sum_{d\mid N}\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{\ord_{N/d}(a)}=\sum_{e\mid N}i_e.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Partition $\ZN$ into strata, apply Corollary~\ref{cor:cycles}, reindex $e=N/d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:prime}
For $p$ prime, $C(p,a)=1+(p-1)/\ord_p(a)=1+i_p$; and for a prime power,
$C(p^k,a)=\sum_{j=0}^k i_{p^j}$.
\end{corollary}

\section{The asymmetric readout at a semiprime}\label{sec:semi}

Let $N=pq$ with $p\ne q$ prime and $\gcd(a,N)=1$.

\begin{theorem}[four strata]\label{thm:four}
The strata of $\Z/pq\Z$ are as follows.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
stratum & cardinality & cycle length & number of cycles\\
\midrule
$S_1$ & $\varphi(N)=(p-1)(q-1)$ & $\ord_N(a)$ & $\varphi(N)/\ord_N(a)$\\
$S_p$ & $q-1$ & $\ord_q(a)$ & $i_q$\\
$S_q$ & $p-1$ & $\ord_p(a)$ & $i_p$\\
$S_N=\{0\}$ & $1$ & $1$ & $1$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:semi}
  C(pq,a)=1+\frac{\varphi(N)}{\ord_N(a)}+\frac{q-1}{\ord_q(a)}
  +\frac{p-1}{\ord_p(a)}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:count} and Proposition~\ref{prop:size}, the
divisors of $pq$ being $1,p,q,pq$.
\end{proof}

The essential point is the cycle-length spectrum
$\{\ord_N(a),\ord_q(a),\ord_p(a),1\}$: the two prime orders appear separately,
on strata of different sizes, and are individually identifiable. The readout is
asymmetric where \eqref{eq:lcm} is symmetric.

\begin{theorem}[factor recovery]\label{thm:factor}
Let $p,q$ be primes and suppose $\ord_q(a)=q-1$. Then the cycle of $\sigma_a$
through the point $p\in\Z/pq\Z$ has length exactly $q-1$, and
$q=(\text{that length})+1$ divides $pq$ with $1<q<pq$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\gcd(p,pq)=p$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:period} the period of $p$ is
$\ord_q(a)=q-1$.
\end{proof}

Thus the readout is a correct factoring algorithm; e.g.\ $N=143$, $a=2$ gives
cycle length $12$ and $\{11,13\}$; $N=221$, $a=7$ gives $16$ and $\{13,17\}$;
$N=899$, $a=3$ gives $30$ and $\{29,31\}$; $N=3127$, $a=2$ gives $58$ and
$\{53,59\}$.

\begin{proposition}[the free stratum is lcm-blind]\label{prop:blind}
If $\gcd(a,N)=\gcd(b,N)=1$ and $\ord_N(a)=\ord_N(b)$, then $\sigma_a$ and
$\sigma_b$ have identical cycle lengths at every point of $S_1$ and the same
number of cycles inside $S_1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{example}[strictness]\label{ex:65}
Let $N=65=5\cdot13$, $a=57$, $b=31$. Then $\ord_{65}(57)=\ord_{65}(31)=4$, so no
unit-group probe distinguishes them. But $\ord_5(57)=4$ while $\ord_5(31)=1$, so
on $S_{13}$ the first permutation has $4$-cycles and the second fixed points.
Even the coarse statistic separates them: $C(65,57)=17$, $C(65,31)=20$.
\end{example}

\section{Three barriers}\label{sec:barriers}

\begin{theorem}[circular entry]\label{thm:circ}
If $x\in\ZN$ has $d=\gcd(x,N)\notin\{1,N\}$, then $d$ is a divisor of $N$ with
$1<d<N$.
\end{theorem}

Trivial as a statement, decisive as a barrier: to read a cycle in a nontrivial
stratum one must possess a point of it, and such a point already yields a
nontrivial factor of $N$ by one Euclidean algorithm. The only stratum reachable
for free is $S_1$, where by Proposition~\ref{prop:blind} the readout is
$\ord_N(a)$ --- the lcm again.

\begin{theorem}[the free stratum exceeds the trial-division range]\label{thm:sqrt}
For distinct primes $p,q\ge3$ one has $\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor<\varphi(pq)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\varphi(pq)=(p-1)(q-1)>pq/2$ for $p,q\ge3$ distinct, while
$\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor^2\le pq$ and $pq\ge15$; combining gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[informative density]\label{thm:density}
Let $p\le q\le 2p$ be primes and $N=pq$. The informative points, i.e.\ those of
$S_p\cup S_q$, number $p+q-1$ and satisfy
\[ (p+q-1)\,\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\ \le\ 6N, \]
so their density is at most $6/\sqrt N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Balance gives $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\le 2p$ and $p+q-1\le 3p$, whence
$(p+q-1)\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\le 6p^2\le 6pq$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:orderfinding}
For every $x$ the period of $x$ divides $\ord_N(a)$; more generally
$\ord_M(a)\mid\ord_N(a)$ whenever $M\mid N$.
\end{proposition}

Hence no cycle length is new: each divides the global order, and determining one
is itself an order-finding problem.

\section{The readout is an aggregate of Pollard probes}\label{sec:burnside}

\begin{lemma}[fixed points]\label{lem:fix}
For any $k$ the permutation $x\mapsto a^kx$ of $\ZN$ has exactly
$\gcd(N,a^k-1)$ fixed points.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$a^kx\equiv x$ iff $N\mid(a^k-1)x$ iff $(N/g)\mid x$ with $g=\gcd(N,a^k-1)$, and
the multiples of $N/g$ in $\ZN$ number exactly $g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Burnside identity]\label{thm:burnside}
Let $L=\ord_N(a)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:burnside}
  L\cdot C(N,a)=\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\gcd\bigl(N,\ a^k-1\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The cyclic group $\langle a\rangle$ of order $L$ acts on $\ZN$ with orbits the
cycles of $\sigma_a$. Burnside's lemma gives
$C=\frac1L\sum_{k<L}|\Fix(a^k)|$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:fix} evaluates each term
(the $k=0$ term being $\gcd(N,0)=N$).
\end{proof}

The summands are exactly the probes of Pollard's $p-1$ algorithm.

\begin{theorem}[minimality criterion]\label{thm:minimal}
With $L=\ord_N(a)$,
\[ L\cdot C(N,a)=N+(L-1)\iff \gcd(N,a^k-1)=1\ \text{for all } 1\le k<L. \]
\end{theorem}

Thus the cycle count exceeds its minimum exactly when some Pollard probe already
produces a nontrivial factor.

\section{The exact information surplus}\label{sec:excess}

\begin{theorem}[index identity]\label{thm:index}
For $N=pq$ with $p\ne q$ prime,
\[ \frac{\varphi(pq)}{\ord_{pq}(a)}
   =\gcd\bigl(\ord_p a,\ \ord_q a\bigr)\cdot i_p\cdot i_q,\qquad
   i_p=\frac{p-1}{\ord_p a},\quad i_q=\frac{q-1}{\ord_q a}. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By \eqref{eq:lcm} and $\lcmop(u,v)\gcd(u,v)=uv$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:evenunit}
For odd primes $p\ne q$ the number $\varphi(pq)/\ord_{pq}(a)$ is even: hence
multiplication by a unit is an even permutation of the unit stratum whenever $N$
has two coprime factors exceeding $2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[excess formula]\label{thm:excess}
For $N=pq$, $p\ne q$ prime,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:excess}
  C(pq,a)=C(p,a)\,C(q,a)+\bigl(\gcd(\ord_p a,\ord_q a)-1\bigr)i_p\,i_q.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute Theorem~\ref{thm:index} into \eqref{eq:semi} and compare with
$C(p,a)C(q,a)=(1+i_p)(1+i_q)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$C(pq,a)\ge C(p,a)C(q,a)$, with equality iff $\gcd(\ord_p a,\ord_q a)=1$. If $a$
is primitive at both primes the surplus is $\gcd(p-1,q-1)-1\ge1$ for odd $p,q$.
\end{corollary}

Since the unit group already reveals the lcm and
$\lcmop\cdot\gcd=\ord_p a\cdot\ord_q a$, the entire additional content of the
ring-level readout is the single number $\gcd(\ord_p a,\ord_q a)$.

\section{The sign at every modulus}\label{sec:sign}

A permutation of an $n$-element set with $c$ cycles has sign $(-1)^{n-c}$, so
the parity of $N-C(N,a)$ is the coarsest summary of the readout.

\begin{theorem}[Zolotarev, cycle-count form]\label{thm:zol}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $\gcd(a,p)=1$. Then $a$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$
iff $i_p=(p-1)/\ord_p(a)$ is even, iff $p-C(p,a)$ is even.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Writing $a=g^t$ for a primitive root $g$, one has $i_p=\gcd(t,p-1)$; Euler's
criterion says $a$ is a square iff $t$ is even, equivalently (as $p-1$ is even)
iff $\gcd(t,p-1)$ is even. Finally $C(p,a)=1+i_p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[parity-dead strata]\label{lem:dead}
If $e=uv$ with $\gcd(u,v)=1$ and $u,v>2$ then $i_e$ is even.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$i_e=\gcd(\ord_u a,\ord_v a)\,i_u i_v$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:index}, and
$\varphi(u),\varphi(v)$ are both even.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[parity along a prime tower]\label{lem:tower}
For odd prime $p$, $\gcd(a,p)=1$ and $k\ge1$: $\ord_{p^k}(a)=\ord_p(a)p^{\,j}$
for some $0\le j\le k-1$, hence $i_{p^k}=p^{\,k-1-j}i_p\equiv i_p\pmod 2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proposition}[divisor-sum parity]\label{prop:sumidx}
For odd $N\ge1$, $\sum_{e\mid N}i_e\equiv 1+\sum_{p\in\mathrm{pf}(N)}i_p\pmod2$,
the sum being over the prime factors of $N$ with multiplicity.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[readout parity]\label{thm:parity}
For odd $N$: $N-C(N,a)\equiv\sum_{p\in\mathrm{pf}(N)}i_p\pmod 2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$N=\sum_{e\mid N}\varphi(e)$ is odd; combine \eqref{eq:count} with
Proposition~\ref{prop:sumidx}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[general Zolotarev--Frobenius law]\label{thm:zolgen}
For every odd $N\ge1$ and every $a$ coprime to $N$,
\[ J(a\mid N)=1\iff N-C(N,a)\ \text{is even}, \]
i.e.\ $\sigma_a$ is an even permutation of $\ZN$ precisely when the Jacobi
symbol is $+1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$J(a\mid N)=\prod_{p\in\mathrm{pf}(N)}(a\mid p)$ and by Theorem~\ref{thm:zol}
each Legendre symbol is $+1$ iff $i_p$ is even; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:parity}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[even modulus]\label{thm:even}
Write $N=2^sm$ with $s\ge1$, $m$ odd, $\gcd(a,N)=1$. Then $N-C(N,a)$ is even
when $s=1$, and for $s\ge2$ its parity equals that of
$i_4=\varphi(4)/\ord_4(a)$, which is odd exactly when $a\equiv3\pmod4$. Thus
$\sigma_a$ is always even when $N\equiv2\pmod4$, and when $4\mid N$ it is odd
exactly when $a\equiv3\pmod4$ --- independently of the odd part $m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The doubling law $i_{2j}=i_j$ for odd $j$ pairs off the divisors $e$ and $2e$,
cancelling their contributions mod $2$. For odd $a$ and $t\ge3$ one has
$\ord_{2^t}(a)\mid 2^{t-2}$, so $i_{2^t}$ is even: the pure $2$-power strata
above $4$ are parity-dead. With Lemma~\ref{lem:dead} for the mixed divisors,
only $e=4$ survives.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[complete sign law]\label{thm:signlaw}
For every $N\ge1$ and every $a$ coprime to $N$, $N-C(N,a)$ is even iff
$J(a\mid N)=1$ when $N$ is odd, and iff ($4\mid N\Rightarrow a\equiv1\pmod4$)
when $N$ is even.
\end{theorem}

Both alternatives are computable in polynomial time from $a$ and $N$ alone: the
sign bit of the readout is free.

\section{Two enlargements of the attack surface}\label{sec:enlarge}

\subsection{A cycle count for arbitrary self-maps}

For $f:\ZN\to\ZN$ define the iteration orbit
$\mathcal O_f(x)=\{f^{[k]}(x):0\le k<N\}$ and let $C_f$ be the number of
distinct such sets. For a permutation of an $N$-element set every orbit closes
within $N$ steps, so $C_f$ is the honest cycle count; for $f=\sigma_a$ one
recovers $C_f=C(N,a)$.

\begin{lemma}[conjugation invariance]\label{lem:conj}
If $e$ is a bijection of $\ZN$ with $e\circ f=g\circ e$, then $C_g=C_f$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction gives $g^{[k]}(e(x))=e(f^{[k]}(x))$, so $\mathcal O_g(e(x))
=e(\mathcal O_f(x))$; $S\mapsto e(S)$ is injective on subsets and carries the
$f$-orbits bijectively onto the $g$-orbits.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Affine maps}

\begin{theorem}[invisible shift]\label{thm:affine}
If $\gcd(a,N)=1$ and $1-a$ is invertible mod $N$, then for every $b$,
$C(x\mapsto ax+b)=C(N,a)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $c=b(1-a)^{-1}$, so $ac+b=c$. Then $e(x)=x+c$ satisfies
$e(ax)=a(x+c)+b$, i.e.\ $e\circ\sigma_a=\sigma_{a,b}\circ e$; apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:conj}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[pure translation]\label{thm:transl}
The translation $x\mapsto x+b$ has exactly $\gcd(N,b)$ cycles, all of length
$N/\gcd(N,b)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[classification of the affine readout]\label{thm:affclass}
Let $A$ be a unit of $\ZN$ and $g=\gcd(N,A-1)$. Then for all shifts $b,b'$,
\[ \gcd(g,b)=\gcd(g,b')\implies C(x\mapsto Ax+b)=C(x\mapsto Ax+b'). \]
In particular $C(x\mapsto Ax+b)=C(N,A)$ whenever $g\mid b$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:affine} is the case $g=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Rescaling by a unit $u$ sends $\sigma_{A,b}$ to $\sigma_{A,ub}$, and translating
by $t$ sends it to $\sigma_{A,b+(A-1)t}$. The cycle count is therefore a
function of the orbit of $b$ under $b\mapsto ub+(A-1)t$; Bézout's identity
realises $g$ inside the ideal generated by $A-1$ and $N$, and that orbit is
exactly $\{b':\gcd(g,b')=\gcd(g,b)\}$. Conclude with Lemma~\ref{lem:conj}.
\end{proof}

Enlarging the one-parameter family $x\mapsto ax$ to the two-parameter family
$x\mapsto ax+b$ therefore buys exactly one additional gcd probe,
$\gcd(N,a-1,b)$, computable in polynomial time without factorisation.

\begin{theorem}[affine sign law]\label{thm:affsign}
For every $N$, every $a$ coprime to $N$ and every $b$,
\[ N-C(x\mapsto ax+b)\ \equiv\ \bigl(N-C(N,a)\bigr)+\bigl(N-\gcd(N,b)\bigr)
   \pmod 2, \]
i.e.\ the affine sign is the product of the multiplicative and translation
signs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Any permutation $\pi$ of a finite set $X$ has
$\mathrm{sign}(\pi)=(-1)^{|X|-\#\mathrm{orbits}(\pi)}$; write
$\sigma_{a,b}=\tau_b\circ\sigma_a$ and use Theorem~\ref{thm:transl}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
At an odd modulus the shift never affects the sign, so
$\mathrm{sign}(\sigma_{a,b})$ corresponds to $J(a\mid N)$ for every $a$ and
every $b$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Power maps}

\begin{theorem}[power readout at a prime]\label{thm:power}
Let $p$ be prime and $k\ge1$ with $\gcd(k,p-1)=1$. Then
\[ C\bigl(x\mapsto x^k\ \text{on }\Z/p\Z\bigr)=C(p-1,k)+1, \]
the right-hand side being the cycle count of $y\mapsto ky$ on $\Z/(p-1)\Z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The discrete logarithm at a primitive root identifies $\Z/p\Z$ with
$\Z/(p-1)\Z$ together with one extra point (the class of $0$), and carries
$x\mapsto x^k$ to $y\mapsto ky$ with that point fixed. Orbit counts are
invariant under conjugation by a bijection, and adjoining a fixed point adds one
orbit.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[power-map sign law]\label{thm:powersign}
For an odd prime $p$ and $\gcd(k,p-1)=1$, the permutation $x\mapsto x^k$ of
$\Z/p\Z$ is even if and only if $4\mid p-1$ implies $k\equiv1\pmod4$.
\end{theorem}

\section{Algorithms}\label{sec:algo}

\begin{description}
\item[A. Stratified cycle count.] For each $d\mid N$ compute $M=N/d$,
$\varphi(M)$, $\ord_M(a)$ and accumulate $\varphi(M)/\ord_M(a)$. Cost:
$\tau(N)$ order computations; available only to someone who already knows the
factorisation.
\item[B. Brute-force readout.] Walk each unvisited $x$ along
$x,ax,a^2x,\dots$ until return. Cost: exactly $N$ map applications, $O(N)$
memory --- the honest cost of the readout.
\item[C. Factoring from an informative point.] Given $x\in S_p$ with $a$
primitive at $q$, return (cycle length of $x$) $+1$. Correct by
Theorem~\ref{thm:factor}; useless by Theorem~\ref{thm:circ}.
\item[D. Burnside cross-check.] Compute $L=\ord_N(a)$ and
$\sum_{k<L}\gcd(N,a^k-1)$; compare with $L\cdot C(N,a)$. Any $k$ with
$1<\gcd(N,a^k-1)<N$ is a successful Pollard probe.
\item[E. Free sign prediction.] Return the parity predicted by
Theorem~\ref{thm:signlaw}: a Jacobi symbol for odd $N$, a residue condition mod
$4$ otherwise. Polynomial time, no factorisation --- a global invariant of a
permutation on $N$ points, predicted without touching it.
\end{description}

\section{Numerical illustrations}

For $N=143$, $a=2$: $\ord_{143}(2)=60$, $\ord_{11}(2)=10$, $\ord_{13}(2)=12$;
strata $120,12,10,1$ carry $2,1,1,1$ cycles of lengths $60,12,10,1$, total
$C=5$. Burnside: $60\cdot5=300=\sum_{k<60}\gcd(143,2^k-1)$, the sum comprising
$143$ at $k=0$, nine hits of value $11$ or $13$, and $1$ elsewhere.

For $N=65$: $C(65,57)=17$ and $65-17$ is even with $J(57\mid65)=+1$;
$C(65,31)=20$ and $65-20$ is odd with $J(31\mid65)=-1$.

For $N=221$, $a=7$: $\ord_{13}(7)=12$, $\ord_{17}(7)=16$, $i_p=i_q=1$,
$\gcd=4$, so \eqref{eq:excess} predicts $2\cdot2+3=7=C(221,7)$.

For $N=15$, $A=4$ ($g=3$): shifts with $\gcd(3,b)=3$ give $9$ cycles, shifts
with $\gcd(3,b)=1$ give $3$; for $A=2$ ($g=1$) all shifts give $5$.

For $p=13$: $k=5$ gives $9=C(12,5)+1$ cycles and $k=7$ gives $10=C(12,7)+1$;
since $4\mid12$, $x\mapsto x^k$ is even exactly for $k\equiv1\pmod4$.

For $N=3127=53\cdot59$ the enumeration touches all $3127$ points while
$\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor=55$; informative points number $111$, density
$0.036\le 6/\sqrt N\approx0.107$.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:disc}

\subsection{What kind of barrier is this?}

The usual vocabulary of hardness --- one-wayness, unstructuredness, generic
lower bounds --- does not describe the situation. The secret is not hidden by
the object: the cycle structure of $\sigma_a$ \emph{displays} $\ord_p(a)$ and
$\ord_q(a)$ separately and permits reading $q$ off a single cycle by a
subtraction. The obstruction is that the object is an enumeration of $N$
elements whose informative region is exactly the set of points that already
constitute a factorisation. One might call this an \emph{access barrier} rather
than an information barrier.

This suggests a sharper formulation for order-based attacks: not ``the readout
is symmetric'' (it is not) but ``every polynomial-time-accessible functional of
the readout is computable from $(N,a)$ alone''.
Sections~\ref{sec:burnside}, \ref{sec:sign} and \ref{sec:enlarge} verify exactly
this for the natural candidates.

\subsection{Placement in the order-probe hierarchy}

Multiplicative orders are \emph{free} as probes (anything computable in
$(\ZN)^\times$, but lcm-flattened), \emph{partial} as constraints on the smooth
parts of $p-1$ and $q-1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:minimal} shows the cycle count is the
aggregate of exactly those constraints), and \emph{sealed} as readouts: the
ring-level permutation separates the individual orders and factors, yet is
sealed behind the barriers of Section~\ref{sec:barriers} and the freeness
results of Sections~\ref{sec:sign}--\ref{sec:enlarge}.

\subsection{Positive by-products}

Theorem~\ref{thm:count} is a closed form for the cycle type of multiplication on
a general residue ring; Theorem~\ref{thm:zolgen} is a Zolotarev--Frobenius
theorem for arbitrary odd moduli, completed at even moduli by
Theorem~\ref{thm:even}, where the sign forgets the odd part of $N$ entirely;
Theorem~\ref{thm:affclass} classifies the affine cycle count by a single gcd;
and Theorem~\ref{thm:power} identifies the power-map readout at a prime with the
multiplicative readout at $p-1$.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A lower bound.} Prove that any algorithm extracting an individual
prime order from the ring-level readout requires $\Omega(N)$ operations in a
model capturing ``iterating the permutation''. The Burnside identity suggests
the right currency: partial sums of Pollard probes.
\item \textbf{A quantum channel.} Is there a quantum procedure whose measurement
statistics see the stratified structure --- the individual $\ord_{N/d}(a)$ ---
rather than only the global $\ord_N(a)$? The strata are not subgroups, so the
hidden-subgroup framework does not apply directly.
\item \textbf{Hint amplification.} All barriers here are hint-free. Given a weak
hint about $p$ or $q$, does the stratified readout amplify it?
Theorem~\ref{thm:density} is the quantitative statement to beat.
\item \textbf{Beyond affine and power families.} Are there cheap-to-specify
permutation families of $\ZN$ whose cycle structure is neither conjugate to a
multiplicative one nor a readout one level down?
\item \textbf{More prime factors.} What is the exact surplus \eqref{eq:excess}
for $N$ with $r$ prime factors, and is there an inclusion--exclusion form of the
``only the gcds are new'' principle?
\item \textbf{Signs of other arithmetic permutations.} Parity localisation
should apply to further families, e.g.\ Möbius transformations on the projective
line over $\ZN$, each time asking whether the resulting invariant is
factorisation-free.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

The permutation $x\mapsto ax$ of $\ZN$ has a completely determined cycle
structure: strata indexed by the divisors of $N$, with sizes $\varphi(N/d)$ and
uniform cycle lengths $\ord_{N/d}(a)$. For a semiprime this separates the two
prime orders into distinct cycle lengths, defeating lcm-blindness, and yields a
correct factoring algorithm. It is nonetheless useless: informative points are
themselves factorisations, the enumeration costs more than trial division,
individual cycle lengths are order-finding problems, the cycle count is an
aggregate of Pollard probes that beats its floor only when a probe already wins,
the surplus over the lcm is exactly one gcd, and every coarse summary --- the
sign at any modulus, the affine extension, the power maps --- is computable in
polynomial time from $N$ and $a$ alone. The asymmetric readout exists, is
exactly understood, and is sealed.

The object of study is the permutation

of the *whole ring* Z/NZ (not merely of its unit group).  The results
demonstrated here are:

         S_d = { x in Z/NZ : gcd(x, N) = d }
     is invariant, has exactly phi(N/d) elements, and every one of its points
     lies on a cycle of length exactly ord_{N/d}(a).  Hence
         #cycles(sigma_a) = sum_{d | N} phi(N/d) / ord_{N/d}(a).

  2. Semiprime readout.  For N = p*q the cycle lengths are exactly
         { ord_N(a), ord_p(a), ord_q(a), 1 }
     on strata of sizes { phi(N), q-1, p-1, 1 }: the individual orders are
     separated, so the readout is strictly finer than the symmetric datum
     ord_N(a) = lcm(ord_p(a), ord_q(a)).

  3. Factoring.  If a is primitive modulo q, the cycle through the point p has
     length q-1, so q = length + 1 is a nontrivial factor of N.

  4. lcm-blindness of the free stratum.  Two multipliers with equal ord_N(a)
     have identical cycle data on the unit stratum -- the only stratum an
     attacker can enter without already knowing a factor.

  5. Burnside identity.  ord_N(a) * #cycles = sum_{k < ord_N(a)} gcd(N, a^k - 1):
     the cycle count is the aggregate of the classical Pollard (p-1) probes.

  6. Excess formula.  #cycles(pq) = #cycles(p) * #cycles(q)
                       + (gcd(ord_p a, ord_q a) - 1) * i_p * i_q,
     where i_r = (r-1)/ord_r(a).

  7. Sign law.  For odd N the permutation sigma_a is even iff the Jacobi symbol
     J(a|N) equals 1; for even N the sign sees only the 2-part of N.

  8. Affine and power readouts.  The shift b in x -> a*x + b changes the cycle
     count only through gcd(gcd(N, a-1), b); the power map x -> x^k on Z/pZ has
     #cycles(x -> k*x on Z/(p-1)Z) + 1 cycles.

  9. Cost barriers.  Enumerating the permutation touches ~N points; the

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# elementary number theory
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def euler_phi(n: int) -> int:
    """Euler's totient phi(n), by trial-division factorisation."""
    result, m, d = n, n, 2
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            while m % d == 0:
                m //= d
            result -= result // d
        d += 1
    if m > 1:
        result -= result // m
    return result


def divisors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All positive divisors of n, in increasing order."""
    small = [d for d in range(1, isqrt(n) + 1) if n % d == 0]
    large = [n // d for d in reversed(small) if n // d != d]
    return small + large


def multiplicative_order(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """ord_n(a): least k >= 1 with a^k = 1 (mod n).  Requires gcd(a, n) = 1."""
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    assert gcd(a, n) == 1, "multiplier must be invertible"
    k, cur = 1, a % n
    while cur != 1:
        cur = (cur * a) % n
        k += 1
    return k


def jacobi_symbol(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Jacobi symbol (a|n) for odd n >= 1, computed by reciprocity."""
    assert n % 2 == 1 and n >= 1
    a %= n
    result = 1
    while a != 0:
        while a % 2 == 0:
            a //= 2
            if n % 8 in (3, 5):
                result = -result
        a, n = n, a
        if a % 4 == 3 and n % 4 == 3:
            result = -result
        a %= n
    return result if n == 1 else 0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# the permutation and its cycle structure
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def cycle_structure(a: int, n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Brute-force cycle-length multiset of x -> a*x on Z/nZ.

    Returns a dict {cycle length: number of cycles of that length}.
    Cost: O(n) -- exactly the enumeration barrier the theory predicts.
    """
    assert gcd(a, n) == 1
    seen = [False] * n
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for start in range(n):
        if seen[start]:
            continue
        length, x = 0, start
        while not seen[x]:
            seen[x] = True
            x = (a * x) % n
            length += 1
        counts[length] = counts.get(length, 0) + 1
    return counts


def cycle_count_bruteforce(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    return sum(cycle_structure(a, n).values())


def cycle_count_formula(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Stratification law: #cycles = sum_{d | n} phi(n/d) / ord_{n/d}(a)."""
    total = 0
    for d in divisors(n):
        m = n // d
        total += euler_phi(m) // multiplicative_order(a % m if m > 1 else 0, m)
    return total


def stratum(n: int, d: int) -> List[int]:
    """S_d = { x in Z/nZ : gcd(x, n) = d }."""
    return [x for x in range(n) if gcd(x, n) == d]


def cycle_length_of_point(a: int, n: int, x: int) -> int:
    """Period of x: theory says it equals ord_{n/gcd(n,x)}(a)."""
    length, y = 0, x
    while True:
        y = (a * y) % n
        length += 1
        if y == x:
            return length


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. stratification law
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_stratification(n: int, a: int) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== Stratification law for N = {n}, a = {a} ===")
    print(f"{'d':>6} {'|S_d| (obs)':>12} {'phi(N/d)':>10} "
          f"{'cycle len (obs)':>16} {'ord_(N/d)(a)':>14}")
    for d in divisors(n):
        s = stratum(n, d)
        m = n // d
        predicted_len = multiplicative_order(a % m, m) if m > 1 else 1
        observed_len = {cycle_length_of_point(a, n, x) for x in s} or {1}
        assert len(observed_len) == 1, "all points of a stratum share one length"
        assert len(s) == euler_phi(m)
        assert observed_len.pop() == predicted_len
        print(f"{d:>6} {len(s):>12} {euler_phi(m):>10} "
              f"{predicted_len:>16} {predicted_len:>14}")
    assert cycle_count_bruteforce(a, n) == cycle_count_formula(a, n)
    print(f"total cycles: {cycle_count_bruteforce(a, n)} "
          f"(formula agrees: {cycle_count_formula(a, n)})")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2 & 3. semiprime readout and factoring
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def semiprime_readout(p: int, q: int, a: int) -> Dict[str, int]:
    """The four data of the readout for N = p*q."""
    n = p * q
    return {
        "ord_N": multiplicative_order(a % n, n),
        "ord_p": multiplicative_order(a % p, p),
        "ord_q": multiplicative_order(a % q, q),
        "cycles": cycle_count_formula(a, n),
    }


def demo_semiprime(p: int, q: int, a: int) -> None:
    n = p * q
    r = semiprime_readout(p, q, a)
    predicted = (1
                 + euler_phi(n) // r["ord_N"]
                 + (q - 1) // r["ord_q"]
                 + (p - 1) // r["ord_p"])
    observed = cycle_count_bruteforce(a, n)
    print(f"\n=== Semiprime readout: N = {p}*{q} = {n}, a = {a} ===")
    print(f"  ord_N(a) = {r['ord_N']} = lcm({r['ord_p']}, {r['ord_q']})   "
          f"(the only datum the unit group exposes)")
    print(f"  cycle lengths by stratum: "
          f"{{S_1: {r['ord_N']}, S_p: {r['ord_q']}, S_q: {r['ord_p']}, S_N: 1}}")
    print(f"  stratum sizes:            "
          f"{{phi(N) = {euler_phi(n)}, q-1 = {q-1}, p-1 = {p-1}, 1}}")
    print(f"  #cycles = 1 + {euler_phi(n)}/{r['ord_N']} + {q-1}/{r['ord_q']}"
          f" + {p-1}/{r['ord_p']} = {predicted}  (brute force: {observed})")
    assert predicted == observed


def factor_via_readout(n: int, p_hint: int, a: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Given a point x = p of a nontrivial stratum, the cycle through it has
    length ord_q(a); if a is primitive mod q this is q-1, so q = length + 1.

def demo_burnside(n: int, a: int) -> None:
    L = multiplicative_order(a, n)
    lhs = L * cycle_count_formula(a, n)
    probes = [gcd(n, pow(a, k, n) - 1 if pow(a, k, n) != 0 else n) for k in range(L)]
    probes[0] = n  # k = 0 gives gcd(N, 0) = N
    rhs = sum(probes)
    print(f"\n=== Burnside identity for N = {n}, a = {a} ===")
    print(f"  ord_N(a) = {L}, #cycles = {cycle_count_formula(a, n)}")
    print(f"  ord_N(a) * #cycles = {lhs}")
    print(f"  sum_k gcd(N, a^k - 1) = {rhs}   (Pollard probes: {probes})")
    nontrivial = [k for k in range(1, L) if 1 < probes[k] < n]
    print(f"  probes that already factor N: k = {nontrivial}")
    assert lhs == rhs

    n = p * q
    op, oq = multiplicative_order(a % p, p), multiplicative_order(a % q, q)
    ip, iq = (p - 1) // op, (q - 1) // oq
    cp = 1 + ip
    cq = 1 + iq
    predicted = cp * cq + (gcd(op, oq) - 1) * ip * iq
    observed = cycle_count_formula(a, n)
    print(f"\n=== Excess formula: N = {p}*{q}, a = {a} ===")
    print(f"  #cycles(p) = {cp}, #cycles(q) = {cq}, "

    print(f"  {cp}*{cq} + ({gcd(op, oq)}-1)*{ip}*{iq} = {predicted}  "
          f"(actual {observed})")
    assert predicted == observed

def cycle_count_map(f, n: int) -> int:
    """Number of cycles of an arbitrary permutation f of {0,...,n-1}."""
    seen = [False] * n
    count = 0
    for start in range(n):
        if seen[start]:
            continue
        count += 1
        x = start
        while not seen[x]:
            seen[x] = True
            x = f(x)
    return count


def demo_affine(n: int, a: int) -> None:
    g = gcd(n, a - 1)
    print(f"\n=== Affine readout for N = {n}, a = {a}  (g = gcd(N, a-1) = {g}) ===")
    base = cycle_count_formula(a, n)
    print(f"  multiplicative count #cycles(x -> a*x) = {base}")
    table: Dict[int, set] = {}
    for b in range(n):
        c = cycle_count_map(lambda x: (a * x + b) % n, n)
        table.setdefault(gcd(g, b), set()).add(c)
    for key in sorted(table):
        assert len(table[key]) == 1, "count depends on b only through gcd(g,b)"
        print(f"  gcd(g, b) = {key:>3}  ->  #cycles = {table[key].pop()}")
    if g == 1:
        print("  1 - a invertible: the shift is completely invisible")
    print("  pure translation x -> x + b has exactly gcd(N, b) cycles: "
          + ", ".join(f"b={b}:{cycle_count_map(lambda x, b=b: (x + b) % n, n)}"
                      f"(gcd={gcd(n, b)})" for b in range(1, min(n, 6))))
    # affine sign law
    for b in range(n):
        lhs = (n - cycle_count_map(lambda x: (a * x + b) % n, n)) % 2
        rhs = ((n - base) + (n - gcd(n, b))) % 2
        assert lhs == rhs
    print("  affine sign law verified: sign(a*x+b) = sign(a*x) * sign(x+b)")


def demo_power_map(p: int) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== Power readout at the prime p = {p} ===")
    for k in range(1, p - 1):
        if gcd(k, p - 1) != 1:
            continue
        observed = cycle_count_map(lambda x: pow(x, k, p), p)
        predicted = cycle_count_formula(k % (p - 1) or 1, p - 1) + 1
        even = (p - observed) % 2 == 0
        law = (not (p - 1) % 4 == 0) or (k % 4 == 1)
        print(f"  k = {k:>3}: #cycles(x -> x^k) = {observed} "
              f"= #cycles(k*x on Z/{p-1}Z) + 1 = {predicted}; "
              f"even permutation: {even} (law: {law})")
        assert observed == predicted and even == law

def demo_barriers() -> None:
    print("\n=== Cost barriers ===")
    print(f"{'N':>8} {'phi(N)':>8} {'points touched':>16} {'sqrt(N)':>9} "
          f"{'informative':>12} {'density':>10}")
    for p, q in [(53, 59), (79, 89), (101, 103), (181, 191)]:
        n = p * q
        touched = n  # every element must be visited to close all cycles
        informative = p + q - 1  # multiples of p or q, excluding 0
        print(f"{n:>8} {euler_phi(n):>8} {touched:>16} {isqrt(n):>9} "
              f"{informative:>12} {informative / n:>10.5f}")
        assert (p + q - 1) * isqrt(n) <= 6 * n  # density <= 6/sqrt(N)
        assert isqrt(n) < euler_phi(n)          # enumeration beats no bound
    print("  informative density <= 6/sqrt(N) for balanced semiprimes:  verified")
    print("  sqrt(N) < phi(N): the free stratum alone is larger than "
          "the trial-division search space")

def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("The stratified cycle readout of x -> a*x on Z/NZ")
    print("=" * 72)

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# elementary number theory
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def euler_phi(n: int) -> int:
    """Euler's totient phi(n), by trial-division factorisation."""
    result, m, d = n, n, 2
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            while m % d == 0:
                m //= d
            result -= result // d
        d += 1
    if m > 1:
        result -= result // m
    return result


def divisors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All positive divisors of n, in increasing order."""
    small = [d for d in range(1, isqrt(n) + 1) if n % d == 0]
    large = [n // d for d in reversed(small) if n // d != d]
    return small + large


def multiplicative_order(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """ord_n(a): least k >= 1 with a^k = 1 (mod n).  Requires gcd(a, n) = 1."""
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    assert gcd(a, n) == 1, "multiplier must be invertible"
    k, cur = 1, a % n
    while cur != 1:
        cur = (cur * a) % n
        k += 1
    return k


def jacobi_symbol(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Jacobi symbol (a|n) for odd n >= 1, computed by reciprocity."""
    assert n % 2 == 1 and n >= 1
    a %= n
    result = 1
    while a != 0:
        while a % 2 == 0:
            a //= 2
            if n % 8 in (3, 5):
                result = -result
        a, n = n, a
        if a % 4 == 3 and n % 4 == 3:
            result = -result
        a %= n
    return result if n == 1 else 0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# the permutation and its cycle structure
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def cycle_structure(a: int, n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Brute-force cycle-length multiset of x -> a*x on Z/nZ.

    Returns a dict {cycle length: number of cycles of that length}.
    Cost: O(n) -- exactly the enumeration barrier the theory predicts.
    """
    assert gcd(a, n) == 1
    seen = [False] * n
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for start in range(n):
        if seen[start]:
            continue
        length, x = 0, start
        while not seen[x]:
            seen[x] = True
            x = (a * x) % n
            length += 1
        counts[length] = counts.get(length, 0) + 1
    return counts


def cycle_count_bruteforce(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    return sum(cycle_structure(a, n).values())


def cycle_count_formula(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Stratification law: #cycles = sum_{d | n} phi(n/d) / ord_{n/d}(a)."""
    total = 0
    for d in divisors(n):
        m = n // d
        total += euler_phi(m) // multiplicative_order(a % m if m > 1 else 0, m)
    return total


def stratum(n: int, d: int) -> List[int]:
    """S_d = { x in Z/nZ : gcd(x, n) = d }."""
    return [x for x in range(n) if gcd(x, n) == d]


def cycle_length_of_point(a: int, n: int, x: int) -> int:
    """Period of x: theory says it equals ord_{n/gcd(n,x)}(a)."""
    length, y = 0, x
    while True:
        y = (a * y) % n
        length += 1
        if y == x:
            return length

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import Literal


def jacobi_symbol(a: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Jacobi symbol (a | n) for odd n >= 1, via quadratic reciprocity."""
    assert n >= 1 and n % 2 == 1
    a %= n
    result = 1
    while a:
        while a % 2 == 0:
            a //= 2
            if n % 8 in (3, 5):
                result = -result
        a, n = n, a
        if a % 4 == 3 and n % 4 == 3:
            result = -result
        a %= n
    return result if n == 1 else 0


def multiplicative_sign(a: int, n: int) -> Literal[1, -1]:
    """Sign of x -> a*x on Z/nZ, predicted in polynomial time."""
    assert gcd(a, n) == 1
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return 1 if jacobi_symbol(a, n) == 1 else -1
    return 1 if (n % 4 != 0 or a % 4 == 1) else -1


def translation_sign(b: int, n: int) -> Literal[1, -1]:
    """Sign of x -> x + b on Z/nZ: it has exactly gcd(n, b) cycles."""
    return 1 if (n - gcd(n, b)) % 2 == 0 else -1


def affine_sign(a: int, b: int, n: int) -> Literal[1, -1]:
    """Sign of x -> a*x + b on Z/nZ, by the affine sign law."""
    return multiplicative_sign(a, n) * translation_sign(b, n)


def power_map_sign(k: int, p: int) -> Literal[1, -1]:
    """Sign of x -> x^k on Z/pZ (p an odd prime, gcd(k, p-1) = 1)."""
    assert gcd(k, p - 1) == 1
    return 1 if ((p - 1) % 4 != 0 or k % 4 == 1) else -1


def _brute_sign(f, n: int) -> int:
    seen = bytearray(n)
    cycles = 0
    for s in range(n):
        if seen[s]:
            continue
        cycles += 1
        x = s
        while not seen[x]:
            seen[x] = 1
            x = f(x)
    return 1 if (n - cycles) % 2 == 0 else -1

<header>
  <h1>The Stratified Cycle Readout Explorer</h1>
  <p>Pick a modulus <em>N</em> and an invertible multiplier <em>a</em>. The map
  x ↦ a·x mod N is a permutation of all of ℤ/Nℤ. Watch how it
  splits into strata indexed by gcd(x, N) — and how each stratum's cycle length is
  the order of a modulo the <em>reduced</em> modulus N/gcd.</p>
</header>

<div class="wrap">
  <div class="controls">
    <label for="preset">Preset modulus</label>
    <select id="preset">
      <option value="11,13">N = 143 = 11 × 13 (the classic)</option>
      <option value="5,13">N = 65 = 5 × 13 (lcm-blind pair lives here)</option>
      <option value="13,17">N = 221 = 13 × 17</option>
      <option value="29,31">N = 899 = 29 × 31</option>
      <option value="3,5">N = 15 = 3 × 5 (tiny)</option>
      <option value="4,15">N = 60 = 2² · 3 · 5 (not a semiprime)</option>
      <option value="1,97">N = 97 (prime: Zolotarev)</option>
    </select>

    <label for="mult">Multiplier a (must be coprime to N)</label>
    <div class="row">
      <input id="mult" type="number" min="1" value="2">
      <button id="next">next valid a →</button>
    </div>
    <input id="slider" type="range" min="1" max="142" value="2">

    <label>Highlight</label>
    <div class="row">
      <button id="hl-none">all strata</button>
      <button id="hl-info">informative only</button>
    </div>

    <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>

    <details>
      <summary>What am I looking at?</summary>
      <div>
        <p>Each dot is one residue class <code>x</code>, placed on a spiral in the order
        0, 1, 2, … N−1. Colour = stratum:</p>
        <p><span class="chip" style="background:#58a6ff"></span>units (gcd = 1)  
           <span class="chip" style="background:#f0883e"></span>multiples of p  
           <span class="chip" style="background:#3fb950"></span>multiples of q  
           <span class="chip" style="background:#bc8cff"></span>zero / other</p>
        <p>Arcs join <code>x</code> to <code>a·x</code>. Every dot of a given colour sits on a
        cycle of the same length, and that length is the order of <code>a</code> modulo
        <code>N/gcd(x,N)</code> — the stratification law.</p>
      </div>
    </details>

    <details>
      <summary>Why this does not break RSA</summary>
      <div>
        <p>To read the orange or green cycles you must first hold an orange or green point.
        But such a point <em>is</em> a nontrivial common divisor with N: one Euclidean
        algorithm and you have already factored N. The only stratum you can enter for free
        is the blue one, whose cycle length is exactly ord<sub>N</sub>(a) =
        lcm(ord<sub>p</sub>a, ord<sub>q</sub>a) — the very datum whose symmetry we were
        trying to escape. Meanwhile the blue stratum alone has φ(N) > √N points.</p>
      </div>
    </details>
  </div>

  <div class="stage">
    <canvas id="cv" width="900" height="520"></canvas>
    <table id="strata">
      <thead><tr><th>stratum S<sub>d</sub></th><th>size (= φ(N/d))</th>
        <th>cycle length (= ord<sub>N/d</sub>(a))</th><th>cycles</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody></tbody>
    </table>
    <div class="verdict" id="formula"></div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="foot">
  Sign law: the permutation is even exactly when the Jacobi symbol J(a|N) = +1 (odd N), and
  exactly when a ≡ 1 (mod 4) or 4 ∤ N (even N). Both are computable from a and N alone —
  no factorisation needed. Try to find a multiplier whose sign contradicts it; you cannot.
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  const cv = document.getElementById('cv'), ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
  const presetEl = document.getElementById('preset');
  const multEl = document.getElementById('mult');
  const slider = document.getElementById('slider');
  const verdict = document.getElementById('verdict');
  const formula = document.getElementById('formula');
  const tbody = document.querySelector('#strata tbody');
  let P = 11, Q = 13, N = 143, A = 2, onlyInfo = false;

  const gcd = (x,y)=>{while(y){[x,y]=[y,x%y];}return x;};
  function phi(n){let r=n,m=n,d=2;while(d*d<=m){if(m%d===0){while(m%d===0)m/=d;r-=r/d;}d++;}
    if(m>1)r-=r/m;return Math.round(r);}
  function ord(a,n){if(n===1)return 1;a=((a%n)+n)%n;if(gcd(a,n)!==1)return 0;
    let k=1,c=a%n;while(c!==1){c=(c*a)%n;k++;if(k>n+2)return 0;}return k;}
  function divisors(n){const s=[];for(let d=1;d*d<=n;d++)if(n%d===0){s.push(d);
    if(d!==n/d)s.push(n/d);}return s.sort((x,y)=>x-y);}
  function jacobi(a,n){a=((a%n)+n)%n;let r=1;while(a){while(a%2===0){a/=2;
    const m=n%8;if(m===3||m===5)r=-r;}[a,n]=[n,a];if(a%4===3&&n%4===3)r=-r;a%=n;}
    return n===1?r:0;}

  function colourOf(x){
    const g = gcd(x,N);
    if(g===1) return '#58a6ff';
    if(g===N) return '#bc8cff';
    if(P>1 && g%P===0) return '#f0883e';
    if(g%Q===0) return '#3fb950';
    return '#bc8cff';
  }

  function draw(){
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,cv.width,cv.height);
    const cx=cv.width/2, cy=cv.height/2;
    const R=Math.min(cx,cy)-24;
    const pos = i => {
      const t = 2*Math.PI*i/N;
      return [cx + R*Math.cos(t-Math.PI/2), cy + R*Math.sin(t-Math.PI/2)];
    };
    // arcs
    ctx.lineWidth = N>400 ? 0.35 : 0.8;
    for(let x=0;x<N;x++){
      const g=gcd(x,N);
      const informative = (g!==1 && g!==N);
      if(onlyInfo && !informative) continue;
      const y=(A*x)%N;
      const [x1,y1]=pos(x), [x2,y2]=pos(y);
      ctx.strokeStyle = colourOf(x) + (informative?'cc':'44');
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(x1,y1);
      ctx.quadraticCurveTo(cx,cy,x2,y2);
      ctx.stroke();
    }
    // dots
    for(let x=0;x<N;x++){
      const g=gcd(x,N);
      const informative = (g!==1 && g!==N);
      if(onlyInfo && !informative) continue;
      const [px,py]=pos(x);
      ctx.fillStyle = colourOf(x);
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(px,py, informative? (N>400?2.2:3.4) : (N>400?1.1:2.0), 0, 2*Math.PI);
      ctx.fill();
    }
  }

  function update(){
    A = Math.max(1, parseInt(multEl.value||'2',10));
    if(gcd(A,N)!==1){
      verdict.innerHTML = '<span class="bad">gcd(a, N) = '+gcd(A,N)+
        ' ≠ 1 — not a permutation. (Also: you just factored N.)</span>';
      tbody.innerHTML=''; formula.textContent=''; draw(); return;
    }
    // strata table
    let rows='', total=0, spectrum=[];
    for(const d of divisors(N)){
      const M=N/d, sz=phi(M), len=ord(A,M)||1, c=Math.round(sz/len);
      total+=c; spectrum.push(len);
      rows += '<tr><td>d = '+d+'</td><td>'+sz+'</td><td>'+len+'</td><td>'+c+'</td></tr>';
    }
    tbody.innerHTML=rows;

    const oN=ord(A,N), oP=P>1?ord(A%P||P,P):0, oQ=ord(A%Q||Q,Q);
    const even = ((N-total)%2===0);
    let predicted;
    if(N%2===1) predicted = (jacobi(A,N)===1);
    else predicted = (N%4!==0) || (A%4===1);

    let msg = '<b>cycle count C(N,a) = '+total+'</b><br>'+
      'cycle-length spectrum: {'+[...new Set(spectrum)].sort((a,b)=>b-a).join(', ')+'}<br>';
    if(P>1 && Q>1 && P!==Q){
      msg += 'ord<sub>N</sub>(a) = '+oN+' = lcm('+oP+', '+oQ+')  —  '+
        'the free probe sees only <b>'+oN+'</b>, the readout sees <b>'+oP+'</b> and <b>'+oQ+
        '</b> separately.<br>';
      if(oQ===Q-1) msg += '<span class="good">a is primitive mod '+Q+
        ': the cycle through the point '+P+' has length '+(Q-1)+', so '+Q+
        ' = length + 1 is a factor.</span><br>';
    }
    msg += 'sign: N − C = '+(N-total)+' is '+(even?'even':'odd')+
      '  ·  predicted free of any factorisation: '+
      (predicted?'even':'odd')+' '+(even===predicted?'<span class="good">✓</span>':
      '<span class="bad">✗</span>');
    verdict.innerHTML = msg;

    let f = 'C(N,a) = ∑<sub>d|N</sub> φ(N/d)/ord<sub>N/d</sub>(a) = '+total+'.';
    if(P>1 && Q>1 && P!==Q && P*Q===N){
      f += '<br>Semiprime form: 1 + φ(N)/ord<sub>N</sub> + (q−1)/ord<sub>q</sub> + '+
           '(p−1)/ord<sub>p</sub> = 1 + '+Math.round(phi(N)/oN)+' + '+
           Math.round((Q-1)/oQ)+' + '+Math.round((P-1)/oP)+' = '+total+'.';
      const g = (function(u,v){return gcd(u,v);})(oP,oQ);
      const ip=Math.round((P-1)/oP), iq=Math.round((Q-1)/oQ);
      f += '<br>Excess over the prime readouts: (gcd(ord<sub>p</sub>, ord<sub>q</sub>) − 1)·i<sub>p</sub>·i<sub>q</sub> = ('+
           g+' − 1)·'+ip+'·'+iq+' = '+((g-1)*ip*iq)+
           '  — the only datum beyond the lcm is that gcd.';
    }
    formula.innerHTML = f;
    draw();
  }

  function setModulus(p,q){
    P=p; Q=q; N=p*q;
    slider.max = Math.max(2, N-1);
    if(gcd(parseInt(multEl.value,10),N)!==1){
      let a=2; while(a<N && gcd(a,N)!==1) a++;
      multEl.value=a; slider.value=a;
    }
    update();
  }

  presetEl.addEventListener('change', ()=>{
    const [p,q]=presetEl.value.split(',').map(Number); setModulus(p,q);
  });
  multEl.addEventListener('input', ()=>{slider.value=multEl.value; update();});
  slider.addEventListener('input', ()=>{multEl.value=slider.value; update();});
  document.getElementById('next').addEventListener('click', ()=>{
    let a=parseInt(multEl.value,10)+1;
    while(a<N && gcd(a,N)!==1) a++;
    if(a>=N) a=1;
    multEl.value=a; slider.value=a; update();
  });
  document.getElementById('hl-none').addEventListener('click',()=>{onlyInfo=false;update();});
  document.getElementById('hl-info').addEventListener('click',()=>{onlyInfo=true;update();});

  setModulus(11,13);
})();
</script>
</body>
</html>

  "interactive_layout": "# The Stratified Cycle Readout — a guided tour

> **The question.** A number $N=pq$ hides two primes. Everything an outsider can compute
> inside the unit group $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$ boils down to one number, the
> multiplicative order $\operatorname{ord}_N(a)$ — and that number is the *least common multiple*
> $\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{ord}_p(a), \operatorname{ord}_q(a))$, which treats $p$ and $q$
> interchangeably. Is there a natural object that pulls the two prime orders apart?
>
> **The answer.** Yes: shuffle *the whole ring*, not just its units. And then discover, step by
> step, why the answer changes nothing.

---

## 1. The shuffle

Fix $N$ and a multiplier $a$ with $\gcd(a,N)=1$. The map

$$\sigma_a : \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}, \qquad \sigma_a(x) = a\,x$$

is a permutation of all $N$ residue classes. Every permutation splits into cycles. The
central discovery is that these cycles are organised by a single arithmetic invariant of a
point: its greatest common divisor with $N$.

For each divisor $d \mid N$ set

$$S_d = \{\, x : \gcd(x,N) = d \,\}, \qquad |S_d| = \varphi(N/d),$$

where $\varphi$ is [Euler's totient function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_totient_function).
Since $\gcd(ax,N)=\gcd(x,N)$, the shuffle keeps each stratum to itself.

**Play with it.** In the widget below, choose a modulus and a multiplier. Colours are strata;
arcs join $x$ to $a\cdot x$. Watch what happens to the orange and green points — the multiples
of $p$ and of $q$ — as you change $a$.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the one-line proof of the stratification law</summary>

The condition $a^k x \equiv x \pmod N$ says $N \mid (a^k-1)x$. Write $d=\gcd(N,x)$, so
$N = dN'$ and $x = dx'$ with $\gcd(N',x')=1$. Cancelling $d$ and using coprimality,

$$N \mid (a^k-1)x \iff N' \mid a^k - 1 \iff a^k \equiv 1 \pmod{N/d}.$$

So the period of $x$ is $\operatorname{ord}_{N/d}(a)$: the point's own gcd with $N$ *cancels part
of the modulus away*. Every point of $S_d$ therefore has the same period, and dividing
$|S_d| = \varphi(N/d)$ by it counts the cycles:

$$\#\mathrm{cycles}(\sigma_a) = \sum_{d \mid N} \frac{\varphi(N/d)}{\operatorname{ord}_{N/d}(a)}.$$

</details>

---

## 2. Seeing the asymmetry

For a semiprime $N = pq$ there are exactly four strata, and the law fills in the whole table:

| stratum | size | cycle length |
|---|---|---|
| $S_1$ (units) | $\varphi(N)=(p-1)(q-1)$ | $\operatorname{ord}_N(a)$ |
| $S_p$ | $q-1$ | $\operatorname{ord}_q(a)$ |
| $S_q$ | $p-1$ | $\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ |
| $S_N=\{0\}$ | $1$ | $1$ |

The two prime orders appear as **separate cycle lengths**. Nothing is flattened. For
$N = 143$, $a=2$ the lengths are $60, 12, 10, 1$ — and $12 = 13-1$, $10 = 11-1$ announce the
factors outright.

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary>Why this is a genuine factoring algorithm (and a concrete separation)</summary>

If $a$ is a primitive root mod $q$ then $\operatorname{ord}_q(a) = q-1$, and the cycle through the
point $p$ lies in $S_p$, so it has length exactly $q-1$: add one and read off $q$. Verified
cases: $N=143$, $a=2 \to \{11,13\}$; $N=221$, $a=7 \to \{13,17\}$; $N=899$, $a=3 \to \{29,31\}$;
$N=3127$, $a=2 \to \{53,59\}$.

And the readout really is *strictly* finer than the lcm. Take $N=65$, $a=57$ and $b=31$: both
have order $4$ modulo $65$, so no unit-group probe separates them — but $\operatorname{ord}_5(57)=4$
while $\operatorname{ord}_5(31)=1$, and the cycle counts are $17$ versus $20$.

</details>

The next algorithm computes the readout the *cheap* way — from the divisor sum, which needs the
factorisation you were trying to find. It is the designer's formula, not the attacker's.

{{algorithm:0}}

And here is the attacker's version: walk every orbit, with no knowledge of $p$ and $q$.

{{algorithm:1}}

---

## 3. Three walls

The readout separates the prime orders and factors $N$. So why is nothing broken? Because of
three obstructions, each provable.

1. **Circular entry.** A point of a nontrivial stratum *is* a nontrivial divisor of $N$: one
   Euclidean algorithm on it already factors $N$. The only stratum you can reach for free is
   the unit stratum — where the cycle length is $\operatorname{ord}_N(a)$, the lcm again.
2. **Cost.** Resolving a permutation of an $N$-element set takes $N$ steps. The unit stratum
   alone has $\varphi(N) > \sqrt{N}$ points, so the readout is worse than trial division and far
   worse than [Pollard's rho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollard%27s_rho_algorithm) at
   $N^{1/4}$. Blind sampling is no better: for balanced semiprimes ($p \le q \le 2p$) the
   informative points satisfy $(p+q-1)\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor \le 6N$, a density of at most
   $6/\sqrt N$.
3. **Order-finding.** Every cycle length divides $\operatorname{ord}_N(a)$; measuring one *is* an
   order computation.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 4. What the shuffle really is

Count the pairs (power $k$, point fixed by $a^k$) two ways — this is
[Burnside's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside%27s_lemma) — and use the fact that
$x \mapsto a^k x$ has exactly $\gcd(N, a^k-1)$ fixed points:

$$\operatorname{ord}_N(a)\cdot \#\mathrm{cycles} \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\operatorname{ord}_N(a)-1}\gcd(N, a^k-1).$$

Those summands are precisely the probes of
[Pollard's $p-1$ algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollard%27s_p_%E2%88%92_1_algorithm).
The cycle count is their aggregate — and it beats its minimum value exactly when one of the
probes already factors $N$ on its own.

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary>How much information is there beyond the lcm? Exactly one number.</summary>

Write $i_p = (p-1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ and $i_q = (q-1)/\operatorname{ord}_q(a)$. Then

$$\#\mathrm{cycles}(pq) = \#\mathrm{cycles}(p)\,\#\mathrm{cycles}(q)
+ \bigl(\gcd(\operatorname{ord}_p a, \operatorname{ord}_q a) - 1\bigr)\,i_p\,i_q .$$

The composite readout is supermultiplicative, with equality exactly when the two prime orders
are coprime. Since the unit group already gives the lcm, and
$\operatorname{lcm}\cdot\gcd = \operatorname{ord}_p a \cdot \operatorname{ord}_q a$, the entire
surplus of the ring-level readout is the single number $\gcd(\operatorname{ord}_p a,
\operatorname{ord}_q a)$.

</details>

Run the exhaustive separation experiment yourself: which pairs of multipliers does the unit
group confuse, and which of those does the readout tell apart?

{{demo:1}}

---

## 5. The free bit: signs

A permutation of $N$ points with $c$ cycles is even or odd according to the parity of $N-c$.
One bit, distilled from the entire spectrum. Surely *that* knows something?

It does not. For a prime modulus this is
[Zolotarev's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zolotarev%27s_lemma): $x\mapsto ax$ is even
on $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ exactly when $a$ is a quadratic residue. The stratified analysis
extends it to all moduli.

> **Sign law.** For every $N$ and every $a$ coprime to $N$, the permutation $x\mapsto ax$ of
> $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ is even if and only if
> the [Jacobi symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_symbol) $J(a\mid N) = +1$ (for $N$
> odd), and — for $N$ even — if and only if $4\mid N$ implies $a\equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

Both conditions are computable in polynomial time from $a$ and $N$ alone, with no
factorisation. You can predict a global invariant of a permutation on $N$ points without ever
touching it.

{{algorithm:3}}

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the parity-localisation proof</summary>

Write $i_e = \varphi(e)/\operatorname{ord}_e(a)$, so $\#\mathrm{cycles} = \sum_{e\mid N} i_e$ and
$N = \sum_{e \mid N}\varphi(e)$. Three facts localise the parity:

* **Parity-dead strata.** If $e = uv$ with $\gcd(u,v)=1$ and $u,v>2$, then
  $i_e = \gcd(\operatorname{ord}_u a, \operatorname{ord}_v a)\,i_u i_v$ is even, because
  $\varphi(u)$ and $\varphi(v)$ are both even.
* **Towers.** For odd $p$, $\operatorname{ord}_{p^k}(a) = \operatorname{ord}_p(a)p^{\,j}$ with
  $j \le k-1$, so $i_{p^k} \equiv i_p \pmod 2$: the parity is constant up a prime tower.
* **Euler's criterion.** $i_p$ is even exactly when $a$ is a square mod $p$.

Hence $N - \#\mathrm{cycles} \equiv \sum_{p \mid N} i_p \pmod 2$ (primes with multiplicity), and
the product of the corresponding Legendre symbols is the Jacobi symbol. At an even modulus a
doubling law $i_{2j}=i_j$ cancels divisors in pairs and the bound
$\operatorname{ord}_{2^t}(a) \mid 2^{t-2}$ kills the $2$-power strata above $4$; only the stratum
$4$ survives, and it carries the character $a \bmod 4$.

</details>

---

## 6. Trying to make the shuffle richer

Two natural enlargements of the attack surface, both closed.

**Affine maps $x\mapsto Ax+b$.** If $1-A$ is invertible, the translation
$x \mapsto x + b(1-A)^{-1}$ conjugates $x\mapsto Ax$ into $x \mapsto Ax+b$ — the same
permutation in different coordinates, so the shift is invisible. In general the cycle count
depends on $b$ **only through $\gcd(\gcd(N,A-1),\,b)$**: one extra gcd, and nothing else. The
pure translation $x \mapsto x+b$ has exactly $\gcd(N,b)$ cycles, and the affine sign is the
product of the multiplicative and translation signs.

**Power maps $x \mapsto x^k$ on $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.** Taking discrete logarithms turns the
power map into multiplication by $k$ on $\mathbb{Z}/(p-1)\mathbb{Z}$, plus the fixed point $0$:

$$\#\mathrm{cycles}(x\mapsto x^k \text{ on } \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}) =
\#\mathrm{cycles}(y \mapsto ky \text{ on } \mathbb{Z}/(p-1)\mathbb{Z}) + 1 .$$

Since $p-1$ is even, the even-modulus sign law applies and gives: $x\mapsto x^k$ is an even
permutation exactly when $4 \mid p-1$ implies $k \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

{{demo:2}}

## 7. Everything at once

The full verification suite below reproduces every claim on concrete numbers: the
stratification law, the semiprime spectrum, factor recovery, lcm-blindness, the Burnside
identity, the excess formula, the sign laws at odd and even moduli, the affine classification,
the power-map identity, and the cost barriers.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 8. The moral

A secret can be *visible* and still be safe. The cycle structure of $x\mapsto ax$ displays
$\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ and $\operatorname{ord}_q(a)$ side by side and lets you read a factor off
a single cycle by subtracting one. Nothing is hidden. What is expensive is the *apparatus*: an
enumeration of $N$ objects whose informative region consists precisely of the points that
already are a factorisation. Call it an access barrier rather than an information barrier — and
note that every accessible summary of the readout (its parity, its affine extension, its
power-map cousins) turns out to be a quantity anyone can compute in polynomial time from $N$
and $a$ alone.

Further reading: [multiplicative order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_order),
[quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_reciprocity),
